Hincmar
hingk'mar
n. (Hincmar, c. 806–882, archbishop of Reims from 845, prosecutor of Gottschalk and author of the Quierzy articles of 853)
Old Frankish personal name, from hin, of uncertain sense, and mar, famous.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hincmar was archbishop of Reims for thirty-seven years and the most powerful churchman of the West Frankish kingdom under Charles the Bald. He is remembered chiefly as the man who silenced Gottschalk of Orbais. At the synod of Quierzy in 849 he had Gottschalk condemned, flogged until he cast his own writings into the fire, and shut up for the rest of his life in the monastery of Hautvillers. In 853 a second synod at Quierzy adopted four articles of Hincmar's drafting: that God predestined the elect to life but did not predestine any to punishment, that the free will lost in Adam is restored by grace, that God wills all men to be saved, and that Christ suffered for all. The church of Lyon answered him, and the synod of Valence in 855 rejected his articles. Hincmar also resisted the forged Pseudo-Isidorean decretals when Pope Nicholas I used them against his authority. The text he leaned on was the universal will of 1Ti 2:4, that God “will have all men to be saved” (1Ti 2:4). The text he could not answer was Christ's own word to unbelievers: “ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep” (John 10:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and predestination as the decree of God by which he has foreordained all things.

expand to see more

SYN'OD, n. In church history, a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.

PREDESTINA'TION, n. The act of decreeing or foreordaining events; the decree of God by which he hath, from eternity, unchangeably appointed or determined whatever comes to pass.

ARCHBISH'OP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class, a metropolitan bishop.

Key Scripture

1Ti 2:4 — "Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth."

John 10:26 — "But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you."

Rom 9:22 — "What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:"

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Modern Corruption

The bishop who answered Augustinian predestination with flogging and four articles of universal grace.

expand to see more

Hincmar's articles are the Carolingian form of the semi-Pelagian settlement, and the dictionary names them so. Predestination to life without any predestination to death leaves the non-elect in a state God did not decree; a universal saving will that does not save leaves God willing what does not come to pass; a death of Christ for all that redeems none in particular empties the purchase of Act 20:28, where the church is the flock God “hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). Rom 9:22 speaks of “the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction” (Rom 9:22) without embarrassment.

The method was worse than the doctrine. A monk who asked to prove his teaching by ordeal was answered with the lash, and the archbishop who would not debate him commissioned John Scotus Eriugena to refute him, and so produced a treatise worse than anything Gottschalk wrote. What is honourable in Hincmar is his resistance to the forged decretals and to papal interference in the Frankish churches. What is mourned is that the West's ablest bishop used his authority to make Augustine's doctrine of grace a crime.

Usage

"“will have all men to be saved” (1Ti 2:4) — the text Quierzy built upon."

"“ye are not of my sheep” (John 10:26) — the text it never answered."

"“purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — a definite flock and a definite price."
